# Z.ai shares its expertise in providing a production service for 'GLM-5.3-Flash' using Chinese-made AI infrastructure, demonstrating how AI agents manage the infrastructure to achieve efficiency equivalent to NVIDIA GPUs.

 Z.ai, a Chinese AI company, has written a blog post explaining how they built their own inference infrastructure to provide the production service for ' 

GLM-5.3-Flash '. Toward Recursive Self-Improvement: How GLM Built Its Own Inference Infrastructure https://z.ai/blog/glm-built-its-inference-infrastructure Providing a high-performance inference service capable of reliably handling production traffic requires extensive system engineering work. For the release of GLM-5.3-Flash, Z.ai built a production-level inference service from scratch on a cluster of over 100,000 Chinese-made AI accelerators. As of the time of writing, all inference processing in the production environment of GLM-5.3-Flash is still running on this system. Regarding this, Z.ai explained, 'This was no easy task. There had never been a case of deploying a cluster of Chinese-made AI accelerators on this scale before. The chips had relatively limited memory capacity and bandwidth, while we needed to support a new model architecture, a 1 million token context window, and multimodal requests. The ecosystem was immature, kernel support was incomplete, and much of what should have been documented had to be done by guesswork. Ultimately, we completed the task. However, this was not accomplished by the team of infrastructure engineers alone. The majority of the work was done by infrastructure agents powered by GLM-5.3.'
...
-Flash. The system went
...
GLM-5.3-Flash underwent live-action testing on OpenCode and OpenRouter under the name Ox-Alpha. Within a week of its launch, GLM-5.3-Flash became the most used AI model on both platforms and reportedly processed over 62 trillion tokens in six days. Z.ai implemented aggressive memory optimization, including a unique method that reduces memory bandwidth consumption by increasing computational load and reduces memory usage for each device by increasing inter-device communication. As a result, it succeeded in building a stack that combines several key techniques, such as linear attention and intra-node tensor parallelism for the LM (Language Model) head, ReplaySSM, W8A8 quantization, mixed-precision cache quantization using INT8/FP8/BF16, and layer partitioning. Furthermore, they introduced an Encode Prefill Decode (EPD) separation architecture. Z.ai reports that these optimizations have resulted in approximately a threefold improvement in end-to-end service performance. Z.ai notes that these improvements have brought hardware utilization efficiency and cost per token to the same level as mainstream NVIDIA GPUs. The infrastructure agent's feedback loop functioned throughout the entire optimization process, allowing GLM-5.3-Flash to go from initial model adaptation to production in less than two weeks. Ultimately, it succeeded in tripling end-to-end throughput compared to the initial baseline. The following figure shows the performance progression of GLM-5.3-Flash from its first run to production. 

 'This process has gradually revealed that the engineering effectiveness of infrastructure agents depends not only on the model's code generation and reasoning capabilities, but also on whether the system can continuously provide useful feedback that allows it to pinpoint specific causes,' Z.ai noted. However, even if an agent understands the entire codebase, it is extremely difficult to determine 'which layer is causing the problem,' 'why the current hypothesis is wrong,' and 'what should be tested next' when receiving feedback such as 'numerical accuracy tests failed,' 'TTFT increased by 30%,' or 'output throughput decreased by 20%' after a change. This is because end-to-end metrics can tell the agent that the results have worsened, but they cannot explain why. Z.ai notes that this necessitated a method for generating granular, root-identifying engineering feedback to directly derive the next action from fragmented end-to-end results. This is also key to building an effective feedback loop for infrastructure agents. Therefore, Z.ai employs 'high-density feedback.' The characteristics of high-density feedback are said to be the following three points: 1: Feedback needs to be sufficiently localized. 2: Feedback needs to be low-cost and readily available. 3. Feedback must support objective verification. By combining these three characteristics, feedback becomes actionable. Feedback on accuracy answers the question, 'Is the calculation correct?' Feedback on system operation reveals, 'Where is the time being spent?' Feedback on performance determines, 'Which method is more effective, and under what conditions is it effective?' In this process, local verification and end-to-end testing play different roles. Local verification helps to eliminate inaccurate or ineffective changes early on and identify candidates worth pursuing, while end-to-end testing verifies whether local outcomes lead to actual service improvements and whether proposed changes introduce new bugs under real workload conditions. Based on these principles, the GLM-5.3-Flash release established an optimization loop involving engineers, infrastructure agents, and a testing environment. Engineers defined goals and system boundaries, agents were responsible for analysis, hypothesis formulation, and code changes, and the testing environment provided layered, timely, and verifiable feedback. 'By working together, the diagnostic process, which previously relied on engineers' experience, was transformed into an engineering workflow that agents can continuously execute,' says Z.ai.
...
Z.ai points out that 'the value of feedback lies not in its quantity, but in whether it helps the agent answer the problem at hand.' He notes that large amounts of unstructured logs can mask important signals, incomplete profiling can lead to misattributions, and optimizations that are effective in microbenchmarks do not necessarily translate to end-to-end performance improvements. He explains that building a feedback environment requires more than just providing test log performance data; it's necessary to clarify what judgments each type of observation can support, what its limitations are, and which conclusions need to be confirmed through further experimentation. Tang Jie, co-founder of Z.ai, also mentioned on X the construction of an inference infrastructure using an infrastructure agent based on GLM-5.3.

signals.excerpt:
Shanghai Artificial Intelligence Laboratory has released Atria Dawn Preview, a 744-billion-parameter open-weight agentic model, without a launch announcement, quietly posting the weights on GitHub and Hugging Face days before publishing the research paper behind it.
...
A GitHub repository named Atria-Dawn-Preview appeared under Shanghai AI Laboratory’s account with no accompanying blog post or announcement. An FP8 checkpoint followed on Hugging Face a day later, alongside a BF16 checkpoint. Only on 14/9/2026 did the lab publish the technical paper behind the release, a 143-author report titled “Atria Dawn: The Dawn of Agentic Superintelligence,” reversing the order in which frontier labs typically publish a paper before shipping weights.
...
The model is released under an MIT licence, permitting unrestricted commercial use, modification and redistribution, terms neither OpenAI nor Anthropic has offered for a flagship model. Shanghai AI Lab also operates a hosted API compatible with the Chat Completions, Messages and Responses formats used by rival providers, so teams running agent stacks built for other vendors can switch by changing an endpoint rather than rewriting integration code.
...
Atria Dawn Preview is a mixture-of-experts model built on top of GLM-5.2, the 744-billion-parameter foundation model Zhipu AI shipped in June 2026 under its own MIT licence, with roughly 40 billion of the total parameters active per token. Shanghai AI Lab further trained that base specifically for extended research and engineering loops: analysing a problem, calling tools, writing and running code, and recovering when an intermediate step fails. The training method, described as a Verifiable Experience Pipeline, ties tool-mediated reasoning to executable environments and outcomes checked externally rather than self-graded.
...
None of Atria Dawn Preview’s benchmark figures have yet been reproduced by an independent evaluator, and the lab has not said what happens after this preview release or when a stable version might follow. The model’s 256,000-token context window is also smaller than rival offerings, and it accepts text only, with no image input. Deploying the model requires hosting between roughly 756 gigabytes and 1.5 terabytes of weights, so the MIT licence removes per-token billing risk while shifting the cost of serving the model onto whoever deploys it.
...
The release lands the same month OpenAI, Anthropic and xAI are engaged in public debate over the pace of frontier development and the guardrails needed around agentic systems with open-ended tool access. Shanghai AI Lab’s decision to publish research-grade weights with no pricing, no guardrail discussion and no formal launch stands in contrast to that conversation. Priced against a hosted rival such as Grok 4.6, which lists at $2 per million input tokens and $6 per million output tokens with a 500,000-token multimodal context window, Atria Dawn Preview carries no listed price at all, since the model is designed to be self-hosted rather than metered.

signals.title: Intel researchers challenge the 1.58-bit limit by optimizing ternary model storage with the new BITCOS format
signals.excerpt:
ternary model storage with
...
The longstanding assumption that 1.58 bits per parameter represents the theoretical "hard floor" for ternary large language model (LLM) quantization has been effectively challenged by a new technical development from Intel. Researchers have introduced a novel storage architecture known as BITCOS, which enables ternary models—those using weights defined as -1, 0, or +1—to operate at an average of 1.485 bits per weight. By fundamentally rethinking how sparse ternary matrices are stored, Intel has achieved a tangible improvement in decoding throughput, recording speed increases of up to 27% on specific hardware configurations. This development signals a significant shift in how engineers manage the memory-to-compute ratio in edge AI deployment.
...
The BITCOS format, an acronym for "BITmap and COmpacted Signs," exploits this sparsity. Instead of storing each weight as a fixed unit, the format divides the data into two distinct, optimized streams. The first stream is a "presence bitmap," where a single bit is assigned to every weight to indicate whether it is zero or nonzero. The second stream stores the actual sign (positive or negative) exclusively for the nonzero weights.
...
This structural separation provides a massive advantage: a zero-value weight now consumes only one bit (the presence flag), while a nonzero weight consumes two
...
(one for the presence flag and one for the sign). Mathematically, the storage cost for the entire model becomes a
...
of the proportion of zeros ($z$).
...
the number of zeros in the model increases, the storage cost drops. For a model with 40% zero weights, the cost is 1.
...
bits; however, as seen in the ternary version of Qwen3-1.7B, which contains over 51% zeros, the cost plummets to 1.485 bits per weight.
...
The development of BITCOS follows a period of rapid experimentation in the field of model compression. Throughout the mid-2020s, the AI community focused heavily on reducing the memory footprint of inference engines to allow powerful models to run on consumer-grade CPUs and integrated GPUs.
...
In recent months, researchers at Intel conducted a comprehensive audit of 29 different ternary model checkpoints across seven distinct model families. ...
The agents try to reproduce the original research from scratch. ...
The agents store that knowledge using something called an MCP, or model context protocol.
...
"An MCP lets AI essentially represent a paper PDF in a form that's easy for agents to access, almost like a filing system," Zou said. Each section of the paper is stored in a different folder, while the introduction, methods, results and conclusion are all organized into a separate file that lives in a parent file of a given paper.
...
AI does the heavy lifting, but Zou and the other human authors still have a role. The manuscript won't capture things like failed experiments or judgment calls behind experimental setups. ...

...

...

...
The release comprises two checkpoints — a full-precision version and an FP8 variant for reduced memory footprint — both under MIT, meaning teams can download, run, fine-tune and deploy the model commercially with minimal restrictions. That licensing choice is the headline for practitioners: unlike many “open” releases that carry usage caveats, an MIT-licensed frontier-scale agent is unusually unencumbered.

# AI tool turns any paper into an ‘agent’ that can collaborate and answer complex queries
The Paper2Agent system makes it easier for researchers to reproduce papers and understand work in unfamiliar fields, authors say.
...
* 
Ka
...
Glickman
...
A new artificial-intelligence tool quickly transforms a research paper into a bespoke AI agent that serves as a “virtual corresponding author”. The agent can respond immediately to questions about the paper, providing a convenient way for scientists to grasp advances in unfamiliar fields. It can also apply the paper’s methods to a fresh data set and even collaborate autonomously with agents for papers from other scientific disciplines.
...
The ability of this tool, called Paper2Agent, to convert static papers into dynamic sources of information “can help us to reimagine what knowledge looks like in the future”, says James Zou, a computer scientist at Stanford University in California and co-author of the paper, which was published today in *Nature*1.
...
Agents are AI assistants that can reason and carry out complex tasks. The Paper2Agent tool starts by accessing a paper’s main text, code, data sets and other elements. The information is deposited onto a digital platform called an MCP server. Then a team of AI agents autonomously builds tools that can apply the paper’s methods to fresh data and places those tools on the server as well.
...
Scientists can then connect to the server using a large language model (LLM) of their choice. This creates a paper-specific agent that can scientists can interact with in plain, conversational language.
...
Zou and his team tested the technology on the paper2 that introduced AlphaGenome, an AI model that predicts the properties of DNA sequences, such as their effect on gene expression. Paper2Agent autonomously created an agent for the AlphaGenome paper in about 45 minutes, and the required computing power cost US$14. The agent passed its initial test with flying colours, answering genetics questions with near-perfect accuracy. The agent also bested the scores of other top biomedical AI agents that were given access to the same paper and asked the same questions. Among the outscored agents was Biomni, a tool developed by academic researchers that draws from dozens of databases but scored far lower than the AlphaGenome agent. Zou says the paper agent’s success comes from its mastery of AlphaGenome’s tools and abilities.
...
Next, the team asked the agent to determine why a single change to a DNA ‘letter’ in a genetic sequence is associated with ‘bad’ cholesterol. The authors asked the agent to identify the precise gene that could explain this link. It identified a gene — a different causal gene to the one pinpointed in the original AlphaGenome paper. Zou says that AlphaGenome’s data on genetic variants support both hypotheses. The discrepancy, he adds, highlights a strength of Paper2Agent: scientists can use the tool to re-evaluate published conclusions without designing entirely new experiments.

Answer: Agentic AI refers to AI systems that can autonomously plan, invoke other tools, and execute tasks multiple times independently. Compared with traditional generative AI, agentic AI requires more frequent data exchange between CPUs, NPUs, memory, and storage devices, thereby placing higher demands on communications efficiency and resource coordination.
...
Q2: What is KV Cache? What are Attention and FFN? What is the purpose of Attention-FFN disaggregation? KV cache stores historical key-value pairs during AI model inference to avoid redundant computation. The longer the context, the more memory it consumes. Attention is a mechanism that captures contextual relationships, while FFNs (Feed-Forward Networks) handle layer-by-layer feature transformation. They are both core computational modules of the Transformer architecture. Attention-FFN disaggregation (AFD) decouples Attention and FFN and deploys them onto different compute units to enable flexible CPU-NPU mixes for different workloads. This improves inference efficiency and resource utilization. AFD is particularly valuable for agentic AI which requires frequent CPU-NPU collaboration.

Shanghai Artificial Intelligence Laboratory's Atria Dawn Preview appeared on Hugging Face and GitHub on September 11 with no blog post, no pricing, and no press release -- just an MIT license and a 143-author paper claiming the top score on five of sixteen agentic benchmarks. No independent lab has measured it yet.
...
Shanghai Artificial Intelligence Laboratory released Atria Dawn Preview, a 744-billion-parameter open-weight agentic model, on September 11 with none of the fanfare that usually accompanies a frontier-scale release: no blog post, no pricing page, no press release. A Hugging Face model card and a matching GitHub repository were the entire announcement; a 143-author technical paper followed three days later, on September 14. The weights ship under the MIT license, meaning any team with enough GPUs can run it without negotiating access with anyone.
...
The model is a mixture-of-experts architecture built on the lab's own 744-billion-parameter GLM-5.2 foundation model -- the same base Z.ai used for its own GLM-5.2 and GLM-5.3 releases, though Atria Dawn Preview is a separate post-training effort, not a Z.ai product. It's trained through what the paper calls a Verifiable Experience Pipeline -- tool-mediated tasks run in real, executable environments and scored against externally verifiable outcomes, rather than the largely static datasets that trained earlier generations. The design targets four agentic domains the lab calls Discovery (research and evidence-gathering), Creation (building software and data visualizations), Delivery (turning results into reports and presentations), and Cybersecurity (finding, validating, and patching vulnerabilities). On the deployment side, the repository ships reference configs for both SGLang and vLLM, an FP8-quantized checkpoint alongside the full-precision BF16 weights for teams without enough memory to run the model at full size, and stated compatibility with the Codex and Claude Code agentic-coding frameworks.
...
On the numbers the lab itself ran, Atria Dawn Preview claims the top score on five of sixteen agentic benchmarks tested, ahead of named rivals that include DeepSeek V4 Pro, Moonshot's Kimi K3, Alibaba's Qwen 3.8 Max, Z.ai's GLM 5.3, OpenAI's GPT-5.6 Sol, and Anthropic's Claude Opus 5. It tops DeepSearchQA at 96.0, BrowseComp at 92.5, CyberGym at 86.5 (versus GLM 5.3's 84.5), and BFCL v4 at 77.0 (versus GLM 5.3's 74.1) -- edging past DeepSeek V4 Pro's 58.3 on SWE-bench Pro with a score of 59.6. On the other eleven benchmarks in the paper's own table, the model is described only as "competitive with frontier agents," not leading -- the paper does not claim a clean sweep, and neither does this account of it. Every one of these numbers comes from the lab's own paper; none has been independently reproduced.
...
The release pattern is itself notable. Where OpenAI's GPT-6 Astra and Anthropic's Claude Opus 5 shipped behind blog posts, pricing pages, and access announcements, Atria Dawn Preview arrived the way an open-source library update does -- a repository going live with no press outreach at all. Combined with the MIT license, that puts a claimed frontier-tier agentic model within reach of any team willing to host 744 billion parameters themselves, with no API waitlist, usage cap, or vendor terms attached -- and it means the model has no first-party hosted price at all: whoever runs it pays only their own compute bill.
...
That combination is worth sitting with for a moment. One of the model's five claimed strengths, per its own paper, is CyberGym -- a benchmark for finding, validating, and patching real software vulnerabilities. A closed lab shipping a strong offensive-security agent behind an API can rate-limit it, log queries, or cut off access; a weights file with no license restriction and no usage terms can't be recalled once it's downloaded. Nothing in the paper or the model card addresses that trade-off directly, and this account isn't asserting the model is dangerous in practice -- only noting that dual-use capability and unrestricted redistribution are two choices the lab made together, not something anyone imposed on it.
...
It's the latest entry in a run of large open-weight releases from Chinese labs this year: Moonshot put Kimi K3's weights on Hugging Face under a Modified-MIT-style license in July, and DeepSeek open-sourced its 305-billion-parameter V4-Flash-Vision-Exp under a straight MIT license in August. signals.title: Intel squeezed a 1.58-bit LLM down to 1.485 bits without changing a single weight — WPS
signals.excerpt:
Intel's BITCOS format compresses ternary model weights below 1.58 bits by exploiting zero-heavy distributions, boosting decoding speed up to 27% on GPUs.

 The New Stack · 2026-09-17 

 

The 1.58 in a 1.58-bit language model sounds like a hard limit, but Intel researchers pushed a ternary model below
...
by changing how its weights are stored rather than changing the model itself.
...
Their new BITCOS format compressed one checkpoint to 1.485 bits per weight and improved decoding throughput by as much as 18% on CPUs and 27% on GPUs.
...
When Intel’s researchers measured the distribution of weights across 29 checkpoints from seven ternary model families, they found that zeros accounted for between 29.7% and 51.5% of the weights. In 26 of those checkpoints, there were enough zeros for BITCOS to beat five-trit packing.
...
The sparsest was a ternary version of Qwen3-1.7B produced with CAT-Q post-training quantization, where 51.48% of the weights were zero, and BITCOS brought the storage cost down to 1.485 bits per weight.
...
Built for token-by-token decoding with small batch sizes, the format reduces the weight data moving through memory. Intel developed separate unpacking kernels for AVX-512 and AVX2 CPUs as well as Xe2 GPUs, joining other efforts to fit compressed models into faster inference pipelines for AI agents.
...
On AVX-512 hardware, the kernel uses the presence bitmap as a mask and `pdep` to scatter the compacted sign bits across the nonzero weight positions. Because Xe2 GPUs lack an equivalent instruction, Intel implemented the same operation with a 2KB lookup table.
...
Compared with the 2-bit kernels, BITCOS ran 10% to 18% faster on the 64-core Xeon server and 2% to 15% faster on the 24-core Core Ultra 9. Performance improved by 9% to 22% on the integrated Arc 140V and by 2% to 27% on the discrete Arc Pro B70. These results measure decoding after the model has loaded, separate from efforts to cut GPU inference cold starts from minutes to seconds.
...
On the eight-core Lunar Lake CPU, Intel’s fixed 2-bit kernel beat BITCOS on every model because the system had enough bandwidth to make unpacking the bottleneck. BITCOS remained faster on the GPUs, although decoding overhead limited the gains. Computer scientist and AI infrastructure author Chip Huyen has made the same point about inference more generally, arguing that the right optimization depends on whether compute, memory or bandwidth is holding back the workload.
...
The paper has not been peer-reviewed; all five test systems used Intel hardware, and the end-to-end benchmarks covered seven models at batch size one. Intel has yet to test the format on Nvidia, AMD, or Arm hardware.
